title: Safe Resemblance, Silent Propagation: Limits of Text-Similarity Guardrails for AI Agent Safety
abstract: When AI agents relay information to one another, an output can preserve an injected instruction's effect on downstream agents even after its wording changes, yet legitimate quotation and template reuse can produce high textual overlap with the source, so text-similarity guardrails that attempt to flag the former risk conflating these two cases. We test this distinction using DonkeyRail, a public classifier combining BLEU, ROUGE-L, and METEOR features, deployed in a controlled three-agent email relay, defining a behavioral measure in which an output counts as functional (the injected procedure induces fresh computations in two subsequent agents) independent of the detector's score, alongside legitimate controls that explicitly authorize quotation and reuse. At its default threshold the classifier misses 8 of 19 functional outputs while flagging 70 of 192 legitimate replies, with every completed quotation and template-reuse reply triggering a false alert; calibrating for low false positives on one template set does not transfer, as the recalibrated threshold detects only one functional output and still produces 15 false alerts on new templates. We also identify an operating-point error in all 21 published classifier configurations, where ROC interpolation replaces direct threshold application, and show formally that high AUC against a surface-level text criterion provides no distribution-free guarantee of high AUC against the behavioral target, while the existing evaluation labels lack the joint observations needed to estimate the gap. An authorization analysis further shows that identical visible transcripts can require different safety decisions depending on the governing policy, a distinction no observation-only classifier can resolve. These results argue for behavioral and policy-grounded evaluation over text-similarity guardrails.
ai_summary: AI agents relay information to one another, an output can preserve an injected instruction's effect on downstream agents . But legitimate quotation and template reuse can produce high textual overlap with the source . We test this distinction using DonkeyRail.

title: Embedding Cosine Measures Text Length Before It Measures Homogenization
abstract: Mean pairwise cosine similarity between transformer embeddings is a standard measure of whether online discourse is converging under generative AI. When the embeddings are mean-pooled outputs of an encoder never trained for sentence similarity, this measure mostly tracks text length. In 6.06 million Reddit comments, an uncentered DeBERTa-v3 measure had suggested that only conservative discourse broke toward homogeneity after late 2022. Truncating the same comments from 10 to 150 words raises their mean cosine by eight times the reported break. A placebo that swaps every comment for a random one of equal length reproduces 81% of the asymmetry, and a fixed-content simulation reproduces 78%. The leading principal direction carries 99.9% of raw DeBERTa homogeneity, and once length is handled the asymmetry disappears under every encoder. On 575,000 Stack Exchange answers the measure reports a post-ChatGPT homogenization of technical sites that the placebo fully reproduces, although answers grew longer. A census of 31 studies locates the risk where anisotropic encoders meet time-series or length-unequal designs. A reverse control on a well-known experiment shows that centering with renormalization can reverse a genuine effect. I propose a low-cost diagnostic protocol. Corrected measures show that the two political camps converged between 2019 and 2022 and stopped converging before ChatGPT. Cross-camp replies engage their targets more closely than same-camp replies.
ai_summary: A placebo that swaps every comment for a random one of equal length reproduces 81% of asymmetry . A fixed-content simulation reproduces 78% of the asymmetry, and the leading principal direction carries 99.9% of raw DeBERTa homogeneity .

title: Lazy-MOSAIC: Accelerating Skill-Centric Manipulation Planning with Learned Skill-Effect World Models
abstract: Long-horizon manipulation tasks require a robot to perform a sequence of physical interactions with its environment, typically combining several different skills. Planning such behaviors efficiently is challenging: given a library of parameterized skills, solutions lie in a vast hybrid space of skill sequences and their parameters, and evaluating each candidate skill's feasibility and effect with a high-fidelity world model such as a physics simulator is computationally expensive. MOSAIC, a recent skill-centric approach, lets the skills guide a non-sequential search toward the regions of this space where they are likely to succeed; however, it pays the full cost of simulation for every parameterized skill it considers. In this work, we introduce Lazy-MOSAIC, a lazy planning framework that instead searches over hypothesized skill outcomes. A cheap learned skill-effect world model predicts, in a fraction of a millisecond, a skill's feasibility and the world state it produces. Lazy-MOSAIC then uses these predictions to focus expensive simulation on promising candidate skills and, when a hypothesis is invalidated, repairs only the affected part of the search, while ensuring that every skill in a returned plan is validated in simulation. We evaluate Lazy-MOSAIC on cluttered-shelf retrieval tasks of increasing difficulty and demonstrate it on a physical robot, showing that it plans substantially faster than baselines with fewer simulator queries, while matching or exceeding their success rate in every setting. Visit skill-mosaic.github.io.
ai_summary: Lazy-MOSAIC lets the skills guide a non-sequential search toward the regions of this space where they are likely to succeed . It pays the full cost of simulation for every parameterized skill it considers .

title: Beyond Leaderboard Ranks: Selecting Software Engineering Agents Under Budget Constraints
abstract: Teams that adopt LLM agents for issue resolution must decide which agent to pay for, and how much to spend finding out. Leaderboard ranks give weak evidence for this decision. Accuracy differences may be statistically unresolved, reported costs may be inconsistent, and evaluating candidate agents can itself be expensive. We investigate budget-constrained agent selection using 58,197 run--task records extracted from the Holistic Agent Leaderboard (HAL), focusing on SWE-bench and six additional benchmarks. Across seven benchmarks, 27 of 35 steps along the accuracy--cost Pareto frontiers are statistically unresolved. On SWE-bench, a run costing $34.16 trails the $170.78 leader by 14.6 percentage points, but the available tasks cannot statistically distinguish their accuracy. Reported costs also differ from standardized token-based estimates by up to 11.7x, while selective task evaluation can bias estimates of full-benchmark execution cost. We therefore compare evaluation strategies under explicit evaluation budgets and deployment-cost caps. Under advance knowledge of task costs, successive halving reaches our uncertainty-aware selection target on SWE-bench using 6.6% of exhaustive evaluation spend, achieving the lowest cost on six of seven benchmarks and tying on the seventh. Its advantage narrows when task costs are unknown before execution or exact-best selection is required. Our findings motivate decision-oriented agent evaluation that accounts for accuracy uncertainty, validates execution costs, and compares complex selection methods against simple adaptive allocation.
ai_summary: Teams that adopt LLM agents for issue resolution must decide which agent to pay for, and how much to spend finding out .

title: Tensorized Automata: Algebraically Informed Representation Learning for Sequential Decision Making
abstract: Task representations for sequential decision making should describe both an objective and progress toward it. We present an algebraically informed pipeline that uses the relational structure and language semantics of alternating finite automata (AFAs) to learn control features and compile compact execution operators. AND-OR message passing learns task and state vectors; selected configurations define an event-driven Boolean matrix operator. We prove that initial and successor language coverage make its carrier represent the exact residual after every prefix, with a sufficient capacity bound in terms of reachable configurations. Conjunction and disjunction use the same pipeline. Fidelity and composition audits evaluate copied formulas and learned disjunct assignments. In five-policy-seed XLand experiments with larger training pools, pooled execution-state vectors outperform raw carrier bits and task-blind conditioning across three task pools under two rejection rewards. They achieve 77.3\% success on multi-event tasks and 99.4\% on a four-task stratum with 33--128-state minimal DFAs, using 16 operator slots. LetterWorld results show useful residual conditioning alongside a remaining gap to RAD. These results connect algebraically informed representation learning to compact task execution and useful policy conditioning.
ai_summary: Task representations for sequential decision making should describe both an objective and progress toward it . We present an algebraically informed pipeline that uses the relational structure and language semantics of alternating finite automata (AFAs) to learn control features and compile compact execution operators .

title: Lower Bounds for the Distributed Computation of Degeneracy and k-Core
abstract: The degeneracy of a graph $G$ is the maximum integer $k$ such that $G$ has a non-empty $k$-core, where the $k$-core is the largest induced subgraph with minimum degree $k$. Computing the $k$-core of a graph $G$ is P-complete. In the decentralized setting, the sequential peeling algorithm can be distributed so that the core value of every node, i.e., the largest integer $k$ for which the node belongs to the $k$-core, is computed in $O(n)$ rounds in $n$-node networks, where adjacent nodes exchange only $O(\log n)$ bits at each round, i.e., in the standard CONGEST model. However, while $Ω(D)$ rounds is a trivial lower bound for these problems in networks of diameter $D$, this does not rule out the existence of an algorithm running in $O(D)+o(n)$ rounds in CONGEST, as it is the case for many very important graph problems, including MST. We show that it is unlikely that such an algorithm exists, or, if it does exist, then it requires $\tildeΩ(\sqrt{n})$ rounds. Specifically, our first main result states that, for any $ε>0$, approximating the degeneracy up to a multiplicative factor $2-ε$ requires $\tildeΩ(\sqrt{n})$ rounds in CONGEST even in networks of diameter $O(\log n)$, and still $\tildeΩ(n^{1/3})$ rounds in networks of constant diameter. We also show that improving this lower bound seems challenging, as we demonstrate that the newer frameworks cannot be used as black boxes to obtain a better lower bound for degeneracy. Our second main result provides a better bound, albeit conditional. It states that, unless the well-known circuit value problem (CVP) admits a parallel polynomial speedup -- an outcome considered unlikely -- it holds that, for every $ε>δ>0$, deciding whether a graph is 2-degenerate cannot be solved in $O(D+ n^{1-ε})$ rounds with $O(n^δ)$-time parallel local computation per round at each node.

title: Almost Controlled: The FDR of Benjamini-Hochberg on Weighted Conformal p-Values
abstract: Weighted conformal p-values generalize conformal inference to cases with covariate shift. One way to use them is to pass them to the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure, either to decide which test units to select or to detect outliers. But weighted conformal p-values may not be positively dependent, so we want to know: does BH still control the false discovery rate (FDR) in finite samples? Based on experiments, it appears to, but we prove it doesn't. We give two counterexamples, certified in exact rational arithmetic, where the FDR exceeds its target level $q$. We also identify how large the difference between the FDR and $q$ can be. With $n$ calibration points, $m$ test units and weight ratio $B$, the relative excess $\mathrm{FDR}/q-1$ is bounded by a function of $n$, $m$, $B$ and $q$ that is of order $\sqrt{Bm/(nq)}$ when $Bm/(nq)$ is small. The bound holds for every configuration with $B\le n$ and every $n$. This order can be reached when multiple non-null test units share a common threshold: in a Poisson-limit model, that configuration's excess is $c(q)\sqrt{Bm/(nq)}$ to first order as $B/n\to0$ and then $m\to\infty$. For some fixed distributions with this structure, the excess decreases only like $n^{-1/2}$ as $n$ grows. If every test unit is null, the excess is $O(B/n)$ at fixed $m$, and in certain configurations it grows linearly with $m$. To assist practitioners in judging how large the FDR can be, we turn that bound, which depends only on $n$, $m$, $q$ and $B$, into a lowered BH level with proved finite-sample control, and give a much less conservative rule of thumb that covers every worst case we were able to find but provides no guarantee.

title: GHySSeg: Real-Time Geometric Ground and Road Segmentation for Hybrid Solid-State LiDAR
abstract: Hybrid solid-state LiDAR sensors are making their way into production vehicles, yet the data they produce differs structurally from that of the established spinning mechanical sensors behind today's autonomous-driving datasets: it is ring-free, dense, cluttered, and concentrated in a frontal field of view. The classical geometric methods that autonomous vehicles rely on for drivable space computation and navigation assume the ordered ring-and-column structure of a 360-degree spinning LiDAR and degrade or fail on this data, while learned alternatives are computationally heavy, hard to certify, and trained almost exclusively on spinning-LiDAR data. We demonstrate that the same dense, per-curve geometry is instead an opportunity to close the divide between the industry's preferred sensors and autonomous-driving research. We present GHySSeg, a purely geometric method that segments ground and drivable road from a single hybrid solid-state LiDAR frame by tracing each scan curve and reading two geometric signatures, a step in height and a fold-back in range, with no training and no graphics processing unit. To evaluate it, we release HySoLiD-Drive, the first public benchmark dedicated to ground and road segmentation on an automotive hybrid solid-state LiDAR, comprising 100 manually labeled and 7000 unlabeled frames recorded by two vehicles in real driving. On this benchmark, GHySSeg surpasses both geometric and learned state-of-the-art baselines across ground and road segmentation, reaching an intersection-over-union of 0.907 for road and 0.896 for ground at over 0.96 precision, while running in real time at about 22 milliseconds per frame on a single core.
ai_summary: Hybrid solid-state LiDAR sensors are making their way into production vehicles . But the data they produce differs structurally from that of the established spinning mechanical sensors . GHySSeg is a purely geometric method that segments ground and drivable road from a single hybrid solid- state LiDar frame .

title: Leverage-Enhanced Sampling Owen Method for Explainable Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Recently, the Shapley value has been widely applied in machine learning for feature importance analysis and model explainability. The multilinear extension of games proposed by Owen (1972) expresses the Shapley value as the integral of partial derivatives along the main diagonal of the cube. Direct evaluation of this integral requires exponential-time computation of the partial derivatives. To improve computational efficiency, we propose a sampling-based estimation strategy within Owen's multilinear extension framework, combining stratified sampling with coalition leverage scores. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces computational costs while maintaining explanation accuracy.
ai_summary: The Shapley value has been widely applied in machine learning for feature importance analysis and model explainability . To improve computational efficiency, we propose a sampling-based estimation strategy .

title: Learning from Duality in Neural Network Field Theories
abstract: We develop neural realizations of positive-level Wess-Zumino-Witten models using bosonic Wakimoto and fermionic Fourier-Berezin fields. Level-rank duality connects the charged sectors of the fermionic construction, where explicit neural observables recover conformal block data and enable the transfer of information about unknown correlators between paired theories. We also show that distinct neural presentations of the same continuum current algebra exhibit different finite-width behavior, with approximation accuracy depending on architecture, regulator, and parameter distribution. These results connect the exact mathematical structure of conformal field theory with the expressive and computational properties of neural field theories.
ai_summary: We develop neural realizations of positive-level Wess-Zumino-Witten models using bosonic Wakimoto and fermionic Fourier-Berezin fields . We also show that distinct neural presentations of the same continuum current algebra exhibit different finite-width behavior .

title: Is This Code Mine? Student Ownership When AI Agents Write the Spec and the Code
abstract: Software engineering courses are starting to ask students to build entire systems with AI coding agents, but little is known about what students actually do with them and whether they still own what they deliver. If the agent writes both the code and the decisions behind it, the artifacts we grade no longer show what students learned. We studied an assignment in which 18 pairs of students built applications with agents under Spec-Driven Development, combining the mined history of their repositories, the prompts they recorded, and a survey of 33 students. The agents wrote 69\% of the specifications meant to keep students in control, sometimes from a prompt of a few words. Students locate their ownership in the ideas, crediting themselves with half of them but a fifth of the code, yet most could not explain that code to a colleague or modify it without the agent, and what they report having written is unrelated to what their own commits declare. The three teams that met the 100,000-line target did so with generated code the application never uses, in one case proposed by the agent itself, and one team rewrote its history to backdate its specifications. Teaching with agents should therefore assess what students specify, review, and can explain, rather than what they ship, and enforce the engineering process with tools rather than trusting it to students or agents.
ai_summary: Software engineering courses are starting to ask students to build systems with AI coding agents . But little is known about what students actually do with them and whether they still own what they deliver . Students locate their ownership in the ideas, crediting themselves with half of them but a fifth of the code .

title: The CYBER-BRIDGE project: An AI-Powered Platform for Cross-Border Cybersecurity, Compliance and Forensics in the EU
abstract: Cross-border cyber attacks on European SMEs and critical-infrastructure operators expose a structural cyber-resilience gap: cybersecurity (threat sharing, detection, response), compliance (framework assessment, certification) and digital forensics (cross-jurisdictional evidence) are jointly regulated by NIS2, the CRA, GDPR and the LED, yet their tooling evolved in silos and rarely interoperates across Member States. The EU-funded CYBER-BRIDGE project integrates the three domains under one architecture and a hash-chained evidence layer: AI-driven CTI sharing with ENISA-aligned notification, multi-framework assessments with retrieval-augmented advisory, and RFC 3161-anchored custody with lawful GDPR/LED exchange, all aligned with MITRE ATT&CK. A sanitised replica of the back-end image hosts a Cyber-Range for upskilling. The contribution is not the individual tools but the reconciliation mechanism that lets one incident produce, from a single evidence record, a cross-border CTI advisory, the regulatory notifications its deadlines demand and a re-verifiable forensic pack; we set out why binding three differently regulated evidence regimes onto one record is non-trivial and how the shared evidence layer resolves the resulting tensions. This paper introduces the project's scope, requirements, pilots, architecture and toolkits; quantitative KPIs follow in later deliverables.
ai_summary: Cross-border cyber attacks on European SMEs and critical-infrastructure operators expose a structural cyber-resilience gap . The EU-funded CYBER-BRIDGE project integrates the three domains under one architecture and a hash-chained evidence layer .

title: Detection-Efficient Watermarking for Vision--Language Agents via Risk-Constrained Strength Allocation
abstract: Vision--language agents generate descriptions, decisions, and instructions that may be reused by users, downstream agents, and automated workflows, creating a need for provenance mechanisms that support content authenticity and post-deployment auditing without unnecessarily degrading response quality. We present a risk-aware semantic watermarking framework that combines predictive uncertainty with a zero-shot multimodal relevance-risk proxy to allocate watermark strength during decoding. A single risk penalty $λ$ exposes a continuous operating frontier, allowing deployment-time selection of a detection--quality trade-off without model retraining. At a selected operating point, mean watermark strength is reduced by approximately 59.4\% relative to fixed-strength watermarking, while perplexity change falls from 0.3634 to 0.1689 and clean/paraphrased ROC-AUC reaches 0.9552/0.9459. A matched-strength analysis shows that this advantage reflects the allocation policy rather than lower average intervention: at comparable mean strength, risk-constrained allocation achieves substantially higher ROC-AUC than fixed, entropy-only, and criticality-only policies, identifying it as detection-efficient rather than quality-dominant. We further show that threshold calibration on finite samples produces substantial false-positive-rate drift, motivating calibration variance reporting as standard practice for auditable provenance.
ai_summary: Vision--language agents generate descriptions, decisions, and instructions that may be reused by users, downstream agents, and automated workflows . We present a risk-aware semantic watermarking framework that combines predictive uncertainty with a zero-shot multimodal relevance-risk proxy .

title: The burden of bacterial antimicrobial resistance in the South Asia and high-income Asia-Pacific region over three decades: a systematic analysis.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is an escalating global public health crisis, yet regional disparities remain poorly characterized. This study systematically assessed AMR burden in South Asia and High-income Asia-Pacific (1990-2021) to inform targeted control strategies. We analyzed data from the Global Burden of Antimicrobial Resistance Study 2021, which serves as the most advanced and current database for assessing the burden of AMR. The study covered 22 pathogens, 84 pathogen-drug combinations, and 11 infectious syndromes in countries and territories across South Asia and High-income Asia-Pacific regions. We quantified the deaths burden under two counterfactual scenarios: deaths associated with AMR and deaths attributable to AMR. In addition, based on these data, we calculated the estimated annual percentage change (EAPC) to evaluate the temporal trends in AMR death rate. In 2021, South Asia recorded approximately 1.26 million (95% UI: 1.11 to 1.42 million) AMR-associated deaths and 334,671 (95% UI: 282,451 to 386,890) AMR-attributable deaths, while the High-income Asia-Pacific region reported 108,668 (95% UI: 92,005 to 125,331) and 23,717 (95% UI: 20,074 to 27,360). AMR-associated death rate declined in South Asia(EAPC: -1.88) but increased in High-income Asia-Pacific (EAPC: 0.74). Over three decades, marked variations emerged across regions and age groups. AMR-associated deaths among children under 5 years declined substantially-by 70% in South Asia and 90% in High-income Asia-Pacific. In contrast, adults 70 + years increased by 155% and 70%, respectively. In 2021, India (69.8 per 100,000) and Japan (65.66 per 100,000) exhibited the highest regional AMR-associated death rates. title: Building a resilient battlefield medical system for future high-tech warfare: key technologies and global health translation prospects.
abstract: Traditional battlefield medical systems demonstrate critical vulnerabilities in highly dynamic, high-threat environments, including inadequate survivability, fragmented treatment chains, and ineffective resource coordination, necessitating a fundamental paradigm shift from the perspective of resilience engineering. This study analyzes these deficiencies across four dimensions, namely damage resistance, response speed, intelligent adaptability, and resource synergy, and integrates artificial intelligence, unmanned platforms, and biomedical frontier technologies to develop a resilient medical system architecture. This architecture incorporates modular distributed deployment, intelligent unmanned support, civil-military integration, and dynamic self-evolution. Its core innovation is the closed-loop integration of physical treatment flows and digital information flows. This transforms the support model from static passive response to dynamic autonomous adaptation. When a node is damaged, the information flow automatically re-routes while the physical flow switches to redundant backup routes to ensure continuity of care. A consortium blockchain-based distributed attestation mechanism guarantees tamper-proof, cross-node trusted sharing of casualty data even in communication-denied combat environments. Meanwhile, operational data continuously feeds back into AI models, promoting iterative optimization of resource pre-positioning strategies. Structurally, the extreme constraints faced by battlefield medicine, namely uncertainty, resource scarcity, and time pressure, are highly similar to those in global health emergencies such as natural disasters and disease outbreaks, making our resilience design principles highly transferable to civilian public health rapid-response systems. Although quantitative simulation validation and ethical reviews for certain emerging technologies remain to be improved, the theoretical framework of this resilience system provides a solid analytical foundation for subsequent empirical quantitative evaluation and cross-scenario practical translation.

This study analyzes these deficiencies across four dimensions, namely damage resistance, response speed, intelligent adaptability, and resource synergy, and integrates artificial intelligence, unmanned platforms, and biomedical frontier technologies .

title: Predicting microvascular invasion in hepatocellular carcinoma using contrast-enhanced CT-based deep learning models: a comparative study of transformer, CNN, and MIL.
abstract: Microvascular invasion (MVI) predicts postoperative recurrence in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), yet preoperative prediction remains challenging. This study compared a Transformer, a convolutional neural network (CNN), and a multiple instance learning (MIL) framework for predicting MVI from contrast-enhanced CT. We retrospectively enrolled 236 patients with pathologically confirmed HCC. Tumor regions of interest were semi-automatically delineated on arterial-phase CT images, and slices centered on the largest tumor cross-section were sampled to build a 2.5D dataset. Four models-Transformer, MIL, CNN, and a clinical baseline-were trained. Models were compared using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) with the DeLong test; bootstrap resampling assessed the stability of AUC estimates. The Transformer achieved the highest AUC of 0.827 (95% CI 0.7585-0.8962), with an accuracy of 0.775, sensitivity of 0.577, and specificity of 0.889, followed by MIL (0.766; 95% CI 0.6875-0.8441), CNN (0.723), and the clinical model (0.715). Bootstrap validation confirmed stable AUC estimates for all models, with the Transformer ranking first (mean 0.827; SD 0.034). The Transformer significantly outperformed the CNN (adjusted P = 0.001) and the clinical model (adjusted P = 0.039); after correction for multiple comparisons, its difference from MIL was of borderline significance (adjusted P = 0.097). No significant differences were observed among the CNN, MIL, and clinical models. Among the four models evaluated, the contrast-enhanced CT-based Transformer predicted MVI most accurately, and its advantage persisted after bootstrap internal validation. These findings concern the ranking of discriminative performance only; the clinical utility of the model is not established, and prospective validation in larger cohorts is required before any clinical application.

title: Hybrid one-shot and vertical federated learning framework for privacy-preserving brain tumor classification and segmentation using the BRISC2025 dataset.
abstract: From MRI images, diagnosis of brain tumors may have limitations due to restriction over patient privacy and lack of annotated datasets so that models cannot be trained across multiple institutions. HOS-VFL: A Hybrid One-Shot and Vertical Federated Learning framework with a two-round protocol that jointly enjoys the advantages of prototype-based one-shot aggregation and encrypted vertical feature space augmentation. Tested on BRISC2025 MRimages of glioma, meningioma, pituitary and non-tumor, with T1-weighted images, expert-annotated, at five simulated institutions, with simulated IID and Dirichlet setups. HOS-VFL obtained values of 98.73% on accuracy and 35-50 for conventional federated learning, with a 94.3% reduction compared to the best baseline valued. HOS-VFL performed 98.73% accuracy and 35-50 for the conventional federated learning with an improvement of 94.3% when compared with its best baseline accuracy. The mean Dice and IoU of Segmentation was 0.9147, 0.8423 respectively. Performance did not wane differently in terms of competitive levels and number of institutions, and was able to withstand gradient inference attacks. HOS-VFL philosophy is centralised performance with minimum communication with retention of raw data local. The method needs to be validated on larger real multi-center datasets before their clinical use.

title: Integrative approaches to acupuncture therapies for post-stroke mild cognitive impairment: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
abstract: Post-stroke mild cognitive impairment (PSMCI) frequently occurs after stroke and substantially restricts patients' functional restoration and overall quality of life. Acupuncture has been widely adopted as an adjunctive intervention; however, the relative efficacy and safety profiles among different acupuncture modalities for PSMCI have not been clearly established. To assess the comparative effectiveness and safety of multiple acupuncture therapies for treating PSMCI via network meta-analysis. RCTs on acupuncture for PSMCI published from their inception to October 2025 were retrieved from nine databases and four clinical trial registries. Study quality was assessed via the Cochrane risk of bias tool. Meta-analysis was performed with ReviewManager and Stata software. In total, 47 RCTs featuring 3,680 participants and 15 types of acupuncture-related interventions were included. Electroacupuncture combined with Moxibustion showed the highest efficacy in improving both MoCA score [MD = 5.42, 95%CI (2.10, 8.74)] and total effective rate. Electroacupuncture plus HBOT [MD = 8.00, 95%CI (5.19, 10.82)] and manual acupuncture plus rTMS [MD = 3.42, 95%CI (0.87, 5.97)] were most effective in improving MMSE. Manual acupuncture plus donepezil [MD = 8.67, 95%CI (5.47, 11.88)] and Electroacupuncture plus cognitive training [MD = -8.09, 95%CI (-10.56, -5.62)] achieved the greatest improvement in Barthel index. Moreover, the adverse events of these interventions were acceptable. This study suggested that acupuncture was effective and safe for PSMCI treatment. title: P2-VGAN: a lightweight velocity-weighted graph attention network for privacy-conscious edge anomaly detection.
abstract: Two persistent challenges hinder intelligent video surveillance in public spaces: dense pixel-based models incur heavy computational costs on edge infrastructure, and continuous capture of identifiable imagery creates substantial visual privacy liabilities. Skeleton-based pipelines, which abstract each video frame into articulated landmark coordinates, support visual data minimization by discarding appearance information. However, conventional graph backbones weight joint trajectories uniformly across time, frequently confusing benign high-speed locomotion (such as sprinting for transit) with violent anomalies. This paper presents the Privacy-Conscious Velocity-Weighted Graph Attention Network (P2-VGAN; the prefix "P2" is retained as a legacy identifier designating privacy-conscious representation rather than a cryptographic guarantee), an efficient framework engineered for desktop-class CPU edge gateways. The pipeline decouples motion analysis from visual appearance by extracting 33 planar body landmarks via a single-shot pose estimator; the application does not intentionally store or transmit decoded RGB frames after pose extraction, ensuring downstream processing operates strictly on appearance-reduced pose coordinates. The primary contribution is the Velocity-Weighted Attention Mechanism (VW-AM), an ultra-lightweight gating module requiring only two shared parameters that converts inter-frame coordinate displacements into a bounded squared-displacement motion proxy. This proxy modulates node features prior to multi-head graph attention, directing message passing toward rapidly moving limbs while damping near-stationary joints. Trained under a weakly supervised Multiple Instance Learning objective with temporal smoothness and sparsity regularizers, P2-VGAN is evaluated across five random seeds on the ShanghaiTech Campus and a human-centric subset of UCF-Crime. On ShanghaiTech, the model achieves a frame-level AUC of 84.72 ± 0.28% with 1.81 M downstream trainable parameters (pose-extractor parameters excluded) and sustains 34.01 frames per second (FPS) on an Intel Core i7-10700 CPU without hardware acceleration. title: Perceptions of AI in veterinary medicine: insights from students, faculty, and practicing veterinarians in Hong Kong.
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) transforms veterinary medicine, understanding stakeholder perceptions is crucial for its effective and responsible integration. To support the development of targeted educational and policy initiatives, this study aimed to evaluate the knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding AI among Bachelor of Veterinary Medicine (BVM) students, PhD students, faculty, and practicing veterinarians in Hong Kong. A cross-sectional online survey was conducted between December 2023 and March 2024 among BVM students, PhD students, and faculty members at City University of Hong Kong, and practicing veterinarians in Hong Kong who are members of the Hong Kong Veterinary Association. The survey assessed participants' familiarity with AI, prior training, perceived benefits, concerns, and willingness to adopt AI in education and clinical practice. Descriptive and comparative analyses were performed to examine differences across stakeholder groups. Of 79 complete responses, nearly half (46.8%) reported unfamiliarity with AI concepts. Only 17.7% had received formal AI training, although 78.5% expressed interest in future AI education. Most respondents agreed that AI could enhance veterinary teaching and practice (83.5%) and 81.0% indicated they would likely incorporate AI tools into their work. Key perceived benefits included support for case-based learning (83.5%), virtual animal models for teaching (77.2%), and improved diagnostic accuracy (74.7%). However, 41.8% felt inadequately prepared to use AI. Major concerns included veterinarian accountability for AI-related harms (79.7%), lack of system flexibility (75.9%), and potential clinical inaccuracies (70.9%). Descriptively, practicing veterinarians reported the lowest AI tool use (66.7% had never used AI tools), the lowest preparedness (66.7% felt unprepared), and lower agreement with AI's clinical benefits, although attitude differences were not statistically significant. These exploratory findings suggest gaps in self-reported AI knowledge and differing perceptions of AI across veterinary stakeholder groups in Hong Kong, with AI use already widespread at the time of the survey despite limited formal training. While enthusiasm for AI integration is high, concerns about preparedness, accuracy, and ethical responsibility remain. Larger, multi-institutional studies are needed to confirm these patterns and to inform targeted training programs and ethical frameworks for safe and effective AI adoption in veterinary medicine.

title: Revisiting dynamic batch scheduling for grokking: the role of batch size, sample budget, and regularization.
abstract: Grokking-the sudden generalization of neural networks long after overfitting-has inspired training strategies aimed at accelerating its onset. This paper revisits dynamic batch size scheduling and asks whether larger batches provide intrinsically better optimization dynamics, or whether they appear better because they process more examples per update. We evaluate three dynamic schedules (linear, exponential, and step-wise increases from 32 to 512) against fixed batch sizes of 32 and 512 across four algorithmic tasks, each with 10 random seeds. When measured by update steps, the fixed-512 baseline is highly competitive: on modular division it reaches 99.6% final accuracy with 10/10 runs grokking at a mean of 3,245 steps. However, this advantage changes substantially after normalizing by total examples processed. Under a matched budget of 240,000 training examples (equivalently 960,000 input tokens), fixed-512 performs poorly and never groks on any task, while smaller-batch and dynamic strategies remain competitive on the modular tasks. A focused hyperparameter sensitivity study additionally shows that grokking depends strongly on weight decay, model size, and maximum batch size: without weight decay, none of the tested strategies grok, while intermediate or strong weight decay can make both fixed-large and dynamic strategies reliable. These results show that larger batches improve update-step efficiency but are not necessarily more sample-efficient, and that their effect is conditional on regularization and capacity. We therefore revise the original interpretation: batch size magnitude is a major confound in grokking experiments, and claims about acceleration should report both update-step and sample-normalized metrics.
